correctness.rationale: The theorem explicitly concerns finite simple trees T with N>=3, and simplices are subsets of vertex-filtration strong gradients: a nonroot vertex points to exactly its sole earlier neighbor, if one exists. Any breadth-first root-first order realizes every one of the N arrows-to-root gradients F_r with N-1 incidence pairs. Any N-1-pair gradient uses all N-1 tree edges and has one unmatched vertex; arrows cannot form a directed cycle or a two-cycle, hence every nonroot arrow leads to that root and the gradient equals F_r. For stars all matched leaf arrows point centrally and at most one arrow leaves the center. For a double star with central edge xy, a central arrow x->a toward a leaf forces x to precede y, whereas y->b would force y to precede x, so they cannot coexist; the remaining central-edge orientation fixes a compatible root. Thus every strong face extends to an F_r at diameter <=3. If diameter>=4, the vertex order v0,v4,v1,v3 on a length-four path yields v1->v0 and v3->v4. The compatible-root sides of the two cut edges are disjoint. This face cannot be part of any top facet and extends to a smaller inclusion-maximal face, establishing nonpurity. Chari-Joswig Proposition 3.1 identifies ordinary top rooted-forest facets, and Donovan-Lin-Scoville Proposition 18 proves strong collapsibility of the ordinary pure tree Morse complex; the result credits this old corollary. Independently re-enumerated every permutation (not merely incremental saved states) for every Prüfer-labeled tree of orders 3,4,5,6 (3+16+125+1296=1440 trees), confirming each maximum gradient set is one of the N rooted orientations and that all strong gradients are root-extendable iff diameter<=3 (300 short-diameter vs 1140 longer-diameter trees). The n=2 boundary is pure with two isolated vertices, so the N>=3 contractibility condition matters. This finite check is corroboration only, not proof of all N.

value.rationale: Purity and extension of filtration gradients to maximum facets are natural intrinsic structural questions for the recently defined strong Morse matching complex. The theorem classifies every finite tree by its graph diameter, distinguishes stars and double stars from all longer trees, and converts a local filtration compatibility restriction into an exact global boundary. The difference between the ordinary forest complex and strong-filtration complex makes the result nontrivial: opposing leafward hub arrows can be ordinary acyclic forest matchings but cannot both be realized in one vertex order. This meaningful exact classification tells researchers precisely when the previously known strong collapse of the ordinary pure tree complex applies to the entire strong complex. It does not claim to classify the homotopy of the nonpure regime or to re-prove old rooted-facet collapse.
residual_risks: The classification does not determine number, dimensions, or homotopy of lower inclusion-maximal faces for diameter >=4.
The collapse consequence is inherited, not an independently new homotopy theorem.
